I hope you don't mind, but I'm going to offer some advice.

If you don't do set-lists, you're probably at least going to want to do an outline. "We'll play this song here and jam for a bit, then we'll work our way to this song."

Pay attention to a clock. 1 hour on, and then a break - seldom more than an hour and sometimes as little as 45 minutes. I usually put 45 minutes of music per set and then that's padded out with 15 minutes of talk. Breaks are then 15 to 30 minutes. A good bar will have a clock that you can see from the stage. Remember, bar clocks are often set 15 minutes early - but your goal is more about playing for a set amount of time.

The reason you do the breaks at a regular interval is to give the people time to go drink. You want them to buy drinks. Your job is to not just entertain - it's to get them to buy booze. By the way, the average length of time is about 15 minutes per drink for the most active purchasers. So, if you make it 15 minutes, they have time to buy one drink and drink it. If you make it 30 minutes then they have time to buy two. If you time it well, they'll be able to buy one, finish it, and buy another just before you're going back on to play.

Again, you're there to entertain AND get them to buy drinks.

Bringing extra guitars is a good idea. You'll want to bring extra strings and you'll eventually probably have a second "gig bag" that's got a bunch of gear in it. You'll learn as you go. You'll want extra strings, picks, spare capo (assuming you use one), a change of clothing, etc... You'll also (strangely enough) probably want extra guitar straps. Believe it or not, they wear out. I've had them wear out while on stage. I'm a very active person on stage, so I carry at least a couple of extra guitar straps. Strange but true. It's a lesson learned from many, many years of experience.

Yes, the lights are hot. LED lights are awesome. Have the bar owner upgrade to LED. It'll lower the temperature by a bunch.

Bring extra clothing. Seriously. Always bring extra clothing. You'll see... Trust me... You want at least two extra shirts and an extra pair of pants. Eventually, you'll probably find yourself buying clothing just to wear on stage. Keep it in good condition and it will last a long time. You'll learn as you go, but most of us like light stuff. It may look like we're wearing a heavy shirt, but it's probably made of a light material.

The position you're (maybe) in is known as "the house band." The house band is the band that plays at that particular bar. They're a regular group of people who play at that specific venue. If they expand, you may find yourself opening for other bands. That's always awesome. I've played with many house bands, usually doing work just for a night or two as a fill-in, but haven't actually been quite a house band. I have been pretty close, but not quite. There's an in-between, where you're playing at that venue on a regular basis - but you don't play there exclusively.

Depending on the venue, you may want a professional demeanor. Bill and write receipts. Keep track - because you're obligated to pay taxes. The venue should also be paying a license fee that allows you to legally play copyright protected work. Many venues do not pay this. It can be a pain in the ass if you get involved, and I'd only imagine it's worse if you're the house band. (I've never had that experience, so I can only guess that it can be pretty rough.)

Groupies... What can I say? Wrap your dick and have fun. However, many of them probably have a boyfriend. This will be drama. When they follow you from place to place, that's awesome. It's great for your ego - but try to not let it go to either head. Man is unfortunate in that we only have enough blood to fill one head at a time. Keep that in mind and take care of protecting yourself. Groupies are awesome - but they bring drama if you sleep with them. They can also do harm to your reputation as a band. This is more true in smaller locations where everyone knows each other.

Try your best to never use equipment that belongs to other people. Use your own gear. The reasons for this are many. One, you know your own gear. Two, your gear is set to do what you tell it to do and you know how to tell it to do it. Three, if you break someone else's gear, you're fucked. It's just a bad idea to use gear belonging to other people. If you end up as the house band and opening for other bands, you'll learn to change out your gear very, very quickly.

There's some general advice and some stuff to consider. You don't have to listen - I'm not your father. However, I have many, many years of experience. All of those are lessons I've learned. I could write for hours about the lessons I've learned.
